title: The core takeaway: Clean bad inputs and log reality over narratives
text: Run would have failed. I switched to a current model and roughly haved its cost by dialing down its internal reasoning. a deprecated library that builds all five agents got migrated and I version locked four dependencies because twice this week a library updated overnight and broke the build with no change from me. Back to the wrong company check. I made it much stronger. Now the AI has to state what role the company name plays in the headline before it decides. That turns a judgment call into a lookup. Accuracy on unseen cases went from 10 out of 16 to 16 out of 16. And it finally works for companies nobody configured by hand. But testing caught something scary. At the old token limit, about one in four of these checks would fail. And on failure, the old code assumed the article was about the company. So shipping the better check would have silently switched it off for a quarter of all headlines while the logs looked perfectly fine.

I flipped the failure to reject, not accept, matching what the instructions already say. When unsure, say no. Last, the monitoring was lying. It stored a handwritten summary of each AI call instead of the real request and response. So, it couldn't answer the one question it exists for. Why did the AI decide that? Now, it logs the real prompt, the real response, real token counts. It was also recording calls that never happened, which inflated our apparent cost. The theme of the week, a confident number can be pure noise. Clean the bad inputs. Make the system fail closed when it's unsure. And log what actually happened, not a story about it. Your turn. Look at one number your own tools report as a fact, a score, a count, a confidence. Ask where it comes from and what happens to it when the data behind it is missing. If the answer is it makes something up, that's your next fix. This week's fixes. More next week. Humanitarians. is AI.
